questions.q: What does the `RECLAIMABLE` column in `docker system df` tell you?
options: The total amount of RAM currently in use
How much of the disk space used by images, containers, or volumes could be freed up by removing things that aren't currently in use
How many containers are currently running
The number of images pulled from Docker Hub this month
questions.explain: RECLAIMABLE shows the portion of each category's disk usage that isn't backing anything currently active -- a strong signal for where cleanup would help most.

options: An image that failed to download completely
An image with no tag pointing to it anymore, typically the previous version left behind after a rebuild reused the same tag
An image that is currently running in a container
An image that has been flagged as malicious by Docker Hub
questions.explain: When you rebuild an image under the same tag (e.g. catalog:latest), the old layers remain on disk but lose their tag, showing up as <none>:<none> -- a dangling image.

questions.q: What is the difference between `docker image prune` and `docker image prune -a`?
options: There is no difference; -a is just a shorthand alias
Without -a, only dangling (untagged) images are removed; with -a, all images not used by any container are removed
docker image prune -a only works on Linux hosts
-a removes containers instead of images
questions.explain: Plain `docker image prune` is conservative and only removes dangling images. Adding -a is more aggressive, removing any image not currently backing a container, tagged or not.

questions.q: Why should you read the warning before confirming `docker system prune -a --volumes`?
options: Because it only removes log files, which is harmless anyway
Because it removes stopped containers, unused networks, unused volumes, and all images without an associated container all at once -- including things you might still need
Because the command cannot be reversed by Docker support
Because it requires administrator password entry
questions.explain: `docker system prune -a --volumes` is the most aggressive built-in cleanup, removing several categories of resources at once -- exactly why Docker shows a warning and asks for confirmation first.

questions.q: Which command would Northbridge's engineers run for routine, low-risk cleanup that never removes an image still backing a container they might restart?
options: docker system prune -a --volumes, run daily
docker container prune and docker image prune (without -a)
docker rm -f on every container regardless of state
There is no way to clean up without risking active resources
questions.explain: docker container prune removes only stopped containers, and plain docker image prune removes only dangling (untagged, unused) images -- both leave anything still in active use untouched.
